full_judgment:
3. The plaintiff Sofia Akhter Alam (since deceased) filed the suit for a decree for ejectment of defendant No.1 from the suit shop claiming that the defendant No. 1 was a defaulter. Her case is that, her mother Rijia Khatoon was owner of the suit shop and the defendant No. 1 was a monthly tenant under her mother since 1st June, 1964. The plaintiff further claims that her mother orally gifted the ground floor of Holding No. 60/1, Purana Paltan to her on 29-8-77 and requested the monthly tenants both verbally and in writing to pay rent to the plaintiff instead of herself. In pursuance to that request, most of the tenants began to pay rent to the plaintiff but the defendant No.1 refused to accept the plaintiff as owner and continued to deposit rent before the House Rent Controller in House Rent Case No. 48 of 1972 in favour of her mother. The plaintiff wanted to start a handicraft business in the suit shop and requested the defendant to hand over vacant possession of the suit shop to her but he refused. Then a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was served on 28-6-83 upon the defendant through Mr. KZM Faruqui requesting the defendant to vacate the possession by 31st July, 1983. The defendant, in spite of receiving the notice on 19-7-83, did not vacate the possession. The plaintiff then filed SCC Suit No. 91 of 1983 which was dismissed for default on 30-9-85. A Miscellaneous case was filed by the plaintiff which was also rejected. Then there was an attempt to settle the dispute amicably but that attempt also failed due to adamant attitude of the defendant. So, the plaintiff again served another notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on 8-11-87 requesting the defendant to vacate possession by 30-11-87 but the defendant did not. The tenancy was terminated by the said notice and the defendant had no legal authority to remain in possession after termination of tenancy. Hence the suit. 

 4. The defendant No. 2, the mother of the plaintiff, appeared in the suit by filing a written statement and supported the case of the plaintiff by admitting that she gifted the suit shop to the plaintiff on 29-8-77. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the material allegations contained in the plaint. His case is that no notice of attornment was served upon him by either the plaintiff or her mother rather her mother continued to withdraw the amount of rent which he deposited in the court of the Rent Controller. He further claims that in 1973 Rijia Khatoon demanded rent at an exorbitant rate from him and, as such, he started depositing rent before the House Rent Controller by filing a case bearing No. 48 of 1973. Rijia Khatoon withdrew the house rent deposited before the House Rent Controller for the last time in December, 1986. The defendant further claims that as the plaintiff could not produce any legal proof that she got the suit shop from her mother on the basis of oral gift and, as such, in spite of their claim and demand, the defendant did not pay any rent to her and he continued to deposit the rent before the House Rent Controller in favour of her mother. The defendant also claims that no possession was delivered to the plaintiff on the basis of the alleged oral gift and no relationship of landlord and tenant was established at any time between him and the plaintiff. He paid rent although by way of deposit before House Rent Controller and was not defaulter. The plaintiff filed this false suit at the instance of her mother to evict him from the suit shop. 

 8. As against the above submission of Mr. Khandakar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Mr. Nurul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff/opposite party No. 1, submits that there is no provision either in the Transfer of Property Act or in any other law now in force about the requirement of serving a notice of attornment. According to him, knowledge of transfer of the ownership on the part of the tenant is sufficient. He contends that in the instant case the defendant was aware of the transfer of ownership from the very beginning and as he had knowledge regarding the change of the ownership, the defendant as a monthly tenant was legally bound to pay rent Ito the plaintiff. He had also submitted that even withdrawal of the house rent by the original owner cannot be a proof that there was no change of ownership and there was no gift. In this connection, he has pointed out that the rent which is deposited before the House Rent Controller would lapse if not withdrawn within 3 years from the date of deposit. Moreover, according to him, withdrawal of rent is not the same thing as acceptance of a person as a tenant. 

 10. Now, let us see whether written notice is necessary or knowledge of the change of the ownership is sufficient. It appears that there is no provision or requirement of serving a notice of attornment after change of ownership. Mr. Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed has also conceded that actually there is no provision for service of notice of attornment. With reference to the case of Madan Lal VS., Manakchand, reported in AIR 1971 (Rajasthan) 55, he has submitted that the word attornment has been borrowed from English law and has not been defined in any law of our country. In the said reported case it appears that both the original owner and the purchaser in writing informed the tenant about the transfer of ownership but I find nothing in the reported case to show that the service of any notice in writing is a legal requirement. The definition of the word attornment has been given by the court in the following words: 

 In this case, the court also made the following observation. 

 12. Now, let us see whether the defendant had knowledge of the change of the ownership. I have already mentioned that the trial Court came to a finding on the basis of the evidence on record that the defendant had such a knowledge. The plaintiff's case is that the defendant was informed of the change of ownership both in writing and verbally. It is true that the plaintiff could not produce the copy of such notice at the time of trial but most of the PWs categorically stated that defendant was informed about the change of the ownership both in writing and verbally. PW I stated this in her examination-in-chief. PW 2 who is the younger brother of the plaintiff, has stated as follows. 

 This is a clear admission on the part of the defendant No. 1 that there was change of the ownership and for that reason some of the original tenants started paying monthly rent to the plaintiff. The above statement also supports the case of the plaintiff that when the monthly tenants were informed about the change of the ownership by both the original owner and the present plaintiff, some of them accepted the plaintiff as the new landlord and others including the defendant No. 1 did not There is no earthly reason to believe that the plaintiff and her mother informed about change of the ownership only to the Nippon Traders and Saidi-Glass House and did not inform the other three tenants including the defendant No. 1. The trial Court, with reference to the entire evidence on record, came to a definite finding that the defendant No. 1 had knowledge of the change of the ownership since 1977. From the evidence on record and from the statements of the DW 1 as quoted above, I am also convinced that defendant No. 1 was fully aware of the change of the ownership from the time of the transfer of the suit shop to the plaintiff by way of oral gift. It appears that the defendant resisted the claim of the plaintiff under some mis-conceptions. He stated as DW 1 that he did not receive any attornment notice but at the same time he also stated that he was bound to pay rent to the plaintiff if she was the owner. I do not understand how he could deny the title of the plaintiff only because he received no attornment notice. When he had full knowledge of the change of the ownership, he was bound to pay rent to the new owner. There is no law requiring service of attornment notice nor there is any specific form for such a notice prescribed by any law. Under such circumstances, the defendant No. 1 cannot deny the ownership of the plaintiff. Had there been a legal requirement of serving such a notice, the defendant could have some justification for denying the ownership of the plaintiff. In view of the above position and evidence on record, I am of the opinion that the learned lower court committed no error of law in holding that the defendant had knowledge of the change in the ownership in favour of the plaintiff and, as such, the defendant was legally bound to pay rent to the plaintiff. 

 15. In this case the gift has been made by a mother in favour of a daughter. For an oral gift, the legal requirements are that there must be an offer and acceptance and there must be also delivery of possession in favour of the donee. In the instant case, the property gifted was in possession of the monthly tenants. So, the question of handing over physical possession of the property does not arise. In such a case, it will be sufficient if the tenants in possession are informed of the gift by the owner and are requested to pay rent to the donee. I have found that such information was given and request was made. 

 16.The present defendant was a monthly tenant under the original owner Rijia Khatoon. He is not legally competent to challenge the gift itself. Mr. Nurul Huq while making his submissions invited my attention to the fact that the donor Rijia Khatoon appeared in the present suit and admitted that she made an oral gift in favour of the plaintiff in 1977 and also delivered possession by requesting the monthly tenants to pay rent to the plaintiff instead of herself. Mr. Nurul Huq also cited the case of Fatal Ahmed vs. Rakhi reported in PLD (Lahore) 218. The donor in the reported case also appeared by filing written statement and admitted that gift. I have been take through the relevant observation of the court as made in paragraph 13 which is reproduced below: 

 "13. In the present case, the rule of Muhammadan Law as to delivery of possession is not being violated if we have regard to the reason of this rule. Here, the donor has supported the gift and not only has he filed a written statement admitting the claim of the plaintiff and praying that a decree be passed in his favour but he has appeared in the witness box.........." 

 Hence, in the instant case also, I find that the donor Rijia Khatoon, appeared by filing written statement and also deposed before the court in support of the claim of the plaintiff and categorically stated that she made oral gift in 1977. The defendant's status is that of a monthly tenant and he not being a claimant of title in the property through the donor and not being a co-sharer in the property through the donor, cannot challenge the validity of the gift. His only right as tenant is that he should be informed of the transfer. We have found that he was informed of the transfer and he had full knowledge of the transfer. Similar decision was also given by the trial Court in the impugned judgment, I find that the learned lower court was not wrong in arriving at such a decision. 

 17. Another ground on which the validity of the impugned judgment and decree has been challenged is that of insufficiency of the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. The notice was issued on 8-11-87 asking the defendant No. 1 to vacate the possession on 30-11-87 on. So, it is obvious that one month's notice as stipulated under the original agreement of 1964 was not served. Mr. Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed is of the view that when clear one month's time was not given by the said notice, the relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant as landlord and tenant cannot be severed and terminated. Mr. Nurul Huq, on the other hand, has submitted that the suit was filed after expiry of 57 days from the date of issue of the notice and, as such, the notice cannot be considered to be insufficient. He is also of the view that the defendant refused to accept the plaintiff as landlord even after he came to know about the change in the ownership and by this denial, the defendant forfeited his right and as a tenant and, as such, even without a notice. The plaintiff can come with a suit for ejectment. Mr. Nurul Huq, in support of his view referred to the case of Maulvi Paiz Bakhsh vs. Syed Shadi Shah reported in PW 1956 (Lahore) 261. It appears that the learned trial Court also found that though clear one month's notice was not issue the suit was filed long after one month from the date of the issue of the notice. In the case cited above, notice was given on 3rd August, 1954 and received by the tenant on 8th August, 1954 and the suit having been instituted on 13th November, 1954, it was held that the suit for ejectment having been filed after 3 months' notice, the defendant was not prejudiced merely because the period mentioned in the notice did not expire with the last date of the month of the tenancy. The principle laid down in this cited case appears to be applicable in the present Case before us and the learned trial Court has actually applied this principle. 

 19. From the above we have found that the defendant No. 1 was informed of the change of the ownership and he had knowledge about transfer of the suit shop to the plaintiff by the original owner. In spite of this knowledge, the defendant denied the title of the plaintiff and refused to accept her as the new owner. It is admitted by both the parties that this denial was made after the gift Admittedly two of the tenants at that time accepted the plaintiff as owner or new landlord and started paying rent to her but the present defendant and two other tenants refused to accept the plaintiff as landlord. It has been settled in so many cases by superior courts of this sub-continent that denial of the title of the owner by the tenant itself will be sufficient for the purpose of obviating the necessity of any notice to vacate. Mr. Huq in this connection also referred to the case of Muhammad Islam Khan vs. Cantonment Board, reported in 1982 Supreme Court Monthly Review, 1056. In this reported case it has been held that the defendant's denial of the plaintiff's title in property can operate as forfeiture and dispense with the notice under section 106 of the TP Act.
